releases.notesHtml:
AI agents can now set up requests themselves, and ask you before anything that changes data.

AI agents (MCP)

  • Describe a request in the call: method, address, parameters, headers, body (JSON, text, form or GraphQL), sign-in and checks. Send it without saving it, change a saved one for one call, or save it.
  • Sign-in set up by the agent: Bearer, Basic, Digest, NTLM, API key, OAuth 2.0 client credentials or password — on a request, or once on a folder (set_folder_auth). Tokens go in secret environment variables (save_environment) and are never shown to the agent again.
  • Performance tests shaped in full: the type, then users or requests per second, duration, ramp up and down, custom stages, think time and targets.
  • You say yes before anything changes data. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS go straight away. A POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE — alone, in a collection run, sent first by another request, or under load — waits for your answer in the agent's window (Claude Code 2.1.76 or later, VS Code). The question comes from the app, so the agent can't answer it for you. With an agent that can't ask, they aren't sent, unless you connect with --allow-changes.
  • New tools: get_request, save_request, set_folder_auth, save_environment. Changes to a request keep its earlier versions in Version history. An agent can't delete anything, and won't change a request whose secret only the app can read.

Plans

  • Settings → Plan: you're on Free during early access, with every feature included. Pro and Team are coming; Tell me when Pro launches gets you one email when they do.

API docs from your collections, API descriptions set up in one place, the app in the tray, resting to free memory, and panes you can resize. Plus updates that ask first, and the command line's version in Settings.

API docs

  • A Docs tab on requests and folders: write a description in Markdown, with a preview.
  • Export → API docs (HTML) makes one page to share or host: a searchable list, each request's description, parameters, headers, body, an example answer, its checks, and curl, JavaScript and Python code. Secrets are left out.
  • Descriptions go out with Postman, OpenAPI and Markdown exports, and come in from Postman, OpenAPI, Insomnia and Bruno.

API descriptions

  • Set up in one place: Ctrl+K → API descriptions shows four steps (added, a folder uses it, requests for its operations, send or run), and each is done from there. Pick a folder, or make a new one, and Use it for this folder.
  • Add the missing requests from the dialog or from the folder's own settings, which show what that folder covers. Requests already in the folder stay and count for their operation; ones that aren't in the description are listed by name.
  • The new requests know where the API runs: when the description gives only a path, the address it was fetched from fills in the rest, or you type it once.
  • Paste its text when an address can't be fetched, say behind a sign-in. Fetching from an address now trusts the same certificates as Send.
  • Find an operation: show all, those with no request, or those with one, and search.
  • A file that isn't an API description says which one and why, with a sample of the format.
  • AI agents (MCP) can see which operations have no request, and add them: list_api_descriptions, api_description_coverage and add_missing_requests.

Running in the background

  • Closing the window keeps the app in the tray while something is running (a request waiting for its answer, a collection run, a performance test, a scheduled check). The tray menu says what's running. Hide to tray from the command palette puts it there on purpose.
  • Settings → Running in the background: keep scheduled checks running (the default), always stay in the tray, or quit. Start with Windows opens into the tray; the installer's last page offers it too, off by default.
  • Resting: when the window has been put away for a while (10 minutes by default) with nothing running, the app rests to free memory and comes back as you left it. Scheduled checks keep running and still notify you.

Test API

  • Resize the panes: drag the line beside Saved requests, and the one between the request and the answer, side by side or one above the other. History, Connections and Compare have one beside their list too. Arrow keys move them; double-click to reset.
  • Drop files on the import, API description and other file dialogs.
  • Guide links in dialogs open the page about what you're doing.

Command line

  • Settings → Command line says whether atc is installed and which version runs. Install puts it on your PATH in one click, no administrator needed.
  • When an older atc from npm comes first, it says New version available: Update, or Use the app's copy, which updates with the app.

Learn

  • A new lesson: OData, the API of business systems (SAP, SuccessFactors, Dynamics): $metadata, $filter, paging, v2 against v4, and what to test, tried on the practice company.
  • Contracts and schemas now checks a whole API against its description, with the practice shop's.

Updates and settings

  • Updates ask first: a check shows what's new; nothing downloads until you say so, then you see its progress and choose to restart now or later.
  • Anonymous usage counts moved to Settings → Privacy. Help links there.

Contract tests, scheduled checks, Salesforce and NetSuite connections, performance tests by type, and a proxy setting. Plus answers shown whole, and a card like this one after every update.

Contract tests

  • Check every answer against your API's OpenAPI file. A folder names an API description, and each answer inside is checked: is the operation in it, is the status documented (error answers too), is the content type, does the body match the documented schema, are required headers there. On Send, in collection runs, on the command line and for AI agents.
  • Importing an OpenAPI file keeps it as the collection's description, so its requests are checked from the start.
  • See which operations have no test yet, and add a request for each in one click.
  • Add a description from a file, a web address, or the practice shop's own, at {{practiceApi}}/openapi.json. Ctrl+K → API descriptions.

Connections

  • Salesforce: sign in with OAuth 2.0 (authorization code or client credentials), browse every queryable object and its fields, and build SOQL with the same builder as OData. Total count, related fields like Owner.Name, and Paste URL take SOQL too.
  • NetSuite: account ID and token-based sign-in (or OAuth 2.0), record types from the metadata catalog, and SuiteQL from the builder, 1,000 rows a page.
  • Names for IDs in NetSuite: a lookup shows its name next to its ID (Asha Rao · 500), and a condition can compare a lookup by its name. Lookups NetSuite won't name show the ID only, and the query still runs.
  • Related data: pick a link's fields as columns, click a record to see all of it as a tree, and edit the filter as text.
  • Export records as CSV or Excel: the ones loaded, or all matching, read page by page (up to 50,000).
  • Save as request keeps a query as a saved request in the folder you pick, signed in by the connection.
  • Practice Salesforce org and NetSuite account in the practice API, so you can try both without a system of your own.

Scheduled checks

  • Run a collection on a schedule while the app is open, from every 5 minutes to every day, with the environment you pick. Run collection → Scheduled checks.
  • A notification when it starts failing, and when it's fixed, saying which request failed and why; or on every failure, every run, or never.
  • Each one shows its last runs as green and red bars, when it runs next, and the last failure in full. Run now, Pause, and it follows its folder when you move it.
  • Download for CI's pipeline has an hourly schedule ready to turn on, for checks while your computer is off.

Performance tests

  • Load tests are now performance tests, in six types: Smoke, Load, Stress, Spike, Soak and Breakpoint. Pick one and the users, duration and stages are set for you.
  • Each report answers its type's question: how it did at the peak (Stress), whether it recovered (Spike), whether it slowed down over time (Soak), and the most it handled before a target broke (Breakpoint).
  • Breakpoint adds users steadily and stops by itself once your targets are missed, or p95 2 s and 5% errors if you haven't set any.
  • On the command line: --preset load and --preset breakpoint.

Requests

  • Answers are shown whole, up to 20 MB (was 64 KB). Very big ones wait behind a panel: show it, show it as plain text, or save it to a file.
  • A Send shows its steps as they happen (Run first, scripts, sign-in, waiting for the host, downloading) with Cancel.
  • New requests wait 5 minutes for an answer (was 60 seconds). When one runs out of time, the answer says how long it waited and offers Wait up to 5m and send again.
  • Production is what you say it is: tick This is production on an environment to get the red edge and the question before changes and performance tests. Nothing is guessed from names.

Settings

  • New sections: Requests (defaults for new requests), Network and proxy, Performance tests (the type new tests start with) and Command line.
  • Proxy: none, the computer's own (HTTPS_PROXY, the default), or one you enter with its sign-in and the hosts that go direct. Used by Send, sign-in, connections, WebSockets, performance tests and the command line. Reach it checks it works.

Updates

  • What's new: after an update the app shows what changed, like this. Open it again any time from About.
  • Important updates say so: they ask you to restart, and say why. Other updates download quietly, show Update ready in the status bar, and install when you close the app.

Look and feel

  • Window buttons match the light and dark themes, and every dialog opens in the middle of the window.
  • Anonymous usage counts are on, with a notice before anything is sent. See exactly what's sent, or turn them off in Settings.

Connections: set a system up once, use it from every request. Plus export, smarter params, and variables you don't have to remember.

Connections

  • A connection is a system set up once — its base URL, sign-in and headers — with a variable like {{successFactors}}. Any request whose address starts with it is sent there with that sign-in. Change the sign-in once and every request follows; nothing to copy into each request.
  • Any sign-in a request can use: Basic, Bearer, API key, OAuth 2.0 (including SAML bearer for SAP SuccessFactors), OAuth 1.0, NTLM, AWS Signature and more. {{names}} in it come from the environment, so one connection serves test and production.
  • Connectors: SAP SuccessFactors, any OData service (v2 and v4), any REST API, and a Practice company to try it without a system of your own.
  • Browse OData systems: their objects with their own names, every field with its label and type, and the records — with conditions, columns (all fields until you pick some), sort, rows at a time, total count, Load more and Copy URL. Open as request opens any query as a request, signed in through the connection.
  • Works on Send, in collection runs, load tests, the command line and for AI agents.

Export

  • Export saved requests — a folder, a few requests, or everything — as APITestCenter, Postman v2.1, OpenAPI 3.1, .http or Markdown. Secrets never go into the file.
  • Double-click an .apitestcenter file and the app opens with it, ready to import.

Requests

  • Type {{ in the address, a param, a header, an auth field or the body: a list of every variable the request can use — connections, folder, environment, saved values, built-in — with their values.
  • Params and headers turn off without being deleted, carry a description, and can all be edited as text with Bulk edit.
  • Right-click a tab: Close, Close others, Close to the right, Close unchanged, Close all, Duplicate, Copy URL.
  • Saved requests: rename (F2), Move to…, drag and drop, several at once, and New request here in a folder.
  • The address that answered is readable and copies on a click. Long dropdowns have a search box.

Installer

  • Running the installer again now says what's on your computer and offers Update, Repair or Uninstall. In the app's colours, and a little quicker.

A new look, projects, and many requests open at once. The biggest update so far.

A new look

  • New logo and colours: lime on graphite, with a light Paper theme. On the Windows taskbar the icon is the hexagon itself.
  • The app's own title bar, in the theme's colours — no grey system bar.
  • A status bar along the bottom: the engine's state, Import, Cookies, Certificates, Mock server, zoom, density, theme, Help and the version.
  • Zoom (Ctrl + / Ctrl − / Ctrl 0) and compact or comfortable rows. Menus and dialogs open smoothly.
  • The app now remembers your theme, zoom, open tabs and environment between restarts (before, a restart forgot them).

Work faster

  • Request tabs: each request opens in its own tab, keeping its answer. Open tabs come back after a restart.
  • Ctrl K finds and runs anything; Ctrl+/ lists every shortcut; Ctrl+B shows or hides the saved requests; Ctrl+, opens Settings.
  • Save sits beside Run load test, with Save as a new request… under its arrow.
  • The response beside the request, or below it — your choice.
  • The environment picker moved to the right of the tabs, with a warning only when a variable is missing.
  • Saved requests: a cleaner panel, a ⋯ menu on requests (Open, Duplicate, Version history, Move to Trash), and right-click on requests and folders.

Safer

  • Environment colours: an environment named like Production turns the top of the window red and asks before a request that changes data, or a load test. Staging-like names are amber.
  • Version history: every save keeps the version it replaces (the last 50). See what changed and restore any version.
  • Trash: deleted requests wait 30 days, with their secrets, and can be restored.

Projects

  • Several projects, each a folder of its own — requests, environments, history — that you can keep in Git. Home lists them, makes new ones, opens folders you already have, and switches between them in a second.

Also

  • Settings in one window: appearance, copy-ready setup for AI assistants (MCP), certificates and cookies, privacy, your files, shortcuts and updates.
  • Import from Bruno (a whole folder, with its environments), .http / .rest files and Hurl, several files at once.
  • Homebrew (macOS) and winget (Windows) packages.
  • Variables can use other variables (baseUrl = https://{{host}}), and imported requests keep their order in collection runs.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• The loading bar now covers the whole wait. It used to finish as soon as the next page appeared, while the page was still loading its data. Now it keeps going until the page's data has arrived, stays long enough to see on fast pages, and is a little thicker.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• Upload files. The Body tab has Form with files (text and file fields, the way web pages upload), File (one file as the whole body — drop it in) and Form (plain form fields). Files are kept in the app's data folder, so saved requests keep working. Load tests upload them too, with test data filled in for each request, and the code the app makes sends them in every language. Try it with the practice API: POST {{practiceApi}}/upload says exactly what arrived.
  • Imports bring forms with files — from Postman, Insomnia, browser recordings, OpenAPI and a pasted curl -F — instead of leaving the body out. Choose the files again; the import says which.
  • Learn — 20 free lessons on APIs, API testing and load testing, from zero, each with something to try in the app, and an A–Z glossary. At apitestcenter.com/learn.
  • A loading bar along the top while a page opens.
  • A smaller installer (about 8 MB less).

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• AI agents can use the app (MCP). Connect Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or Claude Desktop with one line, and ask them to send your requests, run collections and load tests, or read the reports. Secrets stay hidden, and load tests only go to hosts you allow.
  • WebSockets and event streams. Type a ws:// address and press Connect — send and receive messages live. Event-stream (SSE) answers show their events as they arrive. Try both with the practice API.
  • pm.sendRequest in scripts — sign in or look something up from a script, as in Postman. In load tests these extra requests are left out of the numbers.
  • Scripts on folders — write a pre-request or tests script once, for every request inside. Postman collection and folder scripts import to their folders.
  • Earlier answers — a saved request keeps its last 20 answers; open one, or see exactly what changed since (field by field, line by line). Secrets are masked before anything is saved.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• Scripts. A pre-request script and a tests script on every request, with Postman's pm — pm.test, pm.expect, pm.environment.set, pm.response.json(). Tests count like checks, also in collection runs, CI and every request of a load test. Scripts run in a sandbox that can't reach your files, the network or the app.
  • Postman scripts now import — request, folder and collection scripts, as Postman runs them.
  • Mock server. Answer a collection's requests with example responses on your computer, to build a frontend before the API exists. Save as example on any answer, or write one; OpenAPI imports come with examples. Also atc mock for pipelines.
  • OpenAPI imports check the API against its documentation — every request gets a JSON schema check from the documented response.
  • Fix for the command line on Node 23 (Windows): atc suite could end with exit code 127 even when everything passed, failing a pipeline. Please update the npm package.
  • Smoother: the Saved requests panel slides, switching requests fades, and atc ui opens sooner.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• See exactly what was sent. A new Request sent tab shows the request as it went out — after variables, folders, OAuth, signing and cookies — with every header, the body and any redirects. Secrets stay hidden until you choose Show secrets.
  • Copy it as code — curl, PowerShell, JavaScript, Python, C#, Java, Go, or as a ready k6 load-test script.
  • Built-in values: {{$uuid}}, {{$timestamp}}, {{$isoTimestamp}}, {{$randomInt(1,100)}}, {{$randomString}}, {{$randomEmail}}, random names and more — a fresh value for every request, in load tests too. Postman's {{$guid}} and {{$timestamp}} now work as imported.
  • JSON schema checks. Make one from the last response in one click, then every answer must have that shape; a mismatch says where ($.items[0].id should be integer). Plus new checks: more/less than, type, length, patterns, valid JSON, header does not exist.
  • Failed checks say why — got 404, is "pending" — in the app and in CI output.
  • Response cookies in their own tab, and image answers shown as pictures.
  • Running local servers are found reliably in the Base URL picker, with a refresh button.
  • Skip TLS certificate check is now on for new requests, so test servers with their own certificates just work. Requests you saved keep their setting; turn it off to check certificates when testing production.
  • Fixes: typing an address with a port (http://localhost:8080/...) no longer loses the port; atc ui shows the app icon.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• GraphQL. A GraphQL body with a query editor, variables and a schema explorer that loads the API's schema for you. A response with GraphQL errors counts as a failure, in load tests too.
  • Import browser recordings and Insomnia. Bring in a HAR file saved from your browser's developer tools, or an Insomnia export (v4 JSON or v5 YAML) with its folders, environments and auth.
  • atc comes with the desktop app. The Windows installer adds the command line to your PATH (open a new terminal); the Linux .deb adds /usr/bin/atc; on macOS link it once (see the docs). Same version as the app, no Node.js needed.
  • atc ui opens in its own window, and Ctrl+C in the terminal closes it. A browser tab says when it was stopped. --browser opens a tab instead.
  • Fix: an imported request's own Authorization header is kept again, and Use {{token}} as Bearer shows when it should.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• Fix for long load tests with OAuth 2.0. In 0.7.0 a renewed token was never picked up during a load test, so a test longer than the token's life started failing with 401. Each simulated user now renews its token properly — please update if you load-test with OAuth.
  • OAuth 1.0 — for NetSuite token-based authentication and older APIs: consumer and token keys, HMAC-SHA256 or HMAC-SHA1, realm, header or query. Every request gets a fresh signature, in load tests too.
  • More OAuth 2.0 sign-ins: JWT bearer (Salesforce, Google service accounts), SAML bearer (SAP SuccessFactors), and client assertion with a private key and certificate (Azure AD, Okta, Keycloak). The private key never goes to the load generator.
  • Works behind company proxies. The app trusts the certificates your computer trusts — including a proxy's that inspects https — and you can add your company's own CA, instead of switching the certificate check off.
  • Cookie jar. Cookies an API sets are kept and sent back like a browser does, so logins with a session cookie just work — in load tests too. See or delete them under Cookies.
  • Postman import now brings OAuth 1.0, Digest, NTLM, AWS Signature and JWT auth across.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• Folders that sign in once. Collections now nest (Orders/Admin), and a folder can hold auth, headers and variables that every request inside uses. New requests take their folder's sign-in by default. Postman imports keep their folders and folder auth.
  • Every common way to sign in — and it works under load too. OAuth 2.0 (client credentials, password, authorization code with PKCE, tokens renewed by themselves), Digest, NTLM (Windows sign-in), AWS Signature (API Gateway, S3, Lambda URLs), JWTs the app signs with your secret or private key, and client certificates (mutual TLS) per host. Load tests keep tokens fresh and sign every request — long tests don't start failing with 401.
  • Honest numbers with Digest and NTLM. The sign-in exchange is no longer counted as requests or errors in load reports.
  • Auth type is a list with a hint for each, and secrets — client secrets, private keys, passphrases — are kept encrypted on your computer, never in files or exports.
  • Command line: --cert for client certificates in CI; OAuth tokens signed in from the app are reused.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• Everything from the command line — no desktop app needed. npx apitestcenter ui opens the full app in your browser on any folder, so you can build tests on a build server or a locked-down laptop. npx apitestcenter init starts a test folder in your repository with a starter request and a ready GitHub Actions pipeline. Guide: apitestcenter.com/docs/cli-and-ci.html
  • Pick the server, type the path. A Base URL picker sits between the method and the URL. It lists the web addresses in your environment and the web servers running on your computer right now, each with its program and http or https (localhost:5176 · Orders.Api · http). Background services are left out, and nothing leaves your computer.
  • Save an address as a base URL. Sent a request to a full address? One click keeps the server in an environment as {{baseUrl}}, and can switch your other saved requests that use it too.
  • A clearer Compare. Results open full width, with a Comparison tab and a tab for each API's full report. When runs had different load or length, Compare says so, names the odd one out, and doesn't call a winner. Charts mark where a shorter run ended, and the error-rate chart no longer runs past 100%.
  • Dropdowns that match the app, with keyboard support, instead of the operating system's lists.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• Before / after: did your release make it slower? Every report of a request you've run before now compares with your reference run (or the previous one) in one plain sentence — "After is 18% slower", or "About the same" — with every measure marked better, worse, or about the same, and both runs on the same charts. Small run-to-run differences don't count, and a comparison with different load is called unfair instead of judged.
  • Compare any runs, side by side. Add to compare on any report collects runs in a tray at the bottom of the page — different APIs, different days. Compare opens them together, with a tab for each run's full report.
  • Download for CI. On Run collection, one click gives you a zip for your repository: the collection (never secrets), and a ready GitHub Actions pipeline. A new guide walks you through it: apitestcenter.com/docs/ci-walkthrough.html
  • Fail the build when an API gets slower. The command line (npx apitestcenter) gains --baseline, --max-slower, and --save-baseline, with the comparison as its own JUnit test case.
  • Better reports. The HTML export has a Before / after section, lays out cards without gaps, and keeps chart labels readable; the response-time distribution fits its card; words no longer break in the middle.
  • About now links to the user guide.

Already on 0.3.0 or later? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• Run a whole collection. Click ▶ next to a collection, or open Run collection. Every request is sent once, in the order you choose, and you see which passed — and why the others didn't. Save the result as HTML, JUnit (for CI dashboards), or JSON.
  • Pass values from one request to the next. The new Save values tab takes a value from an answer — like the id of a new order — as {{orderId}} for the requests after it. Works in collection runs and between Sends.
  • Honest reports when you're blocked. If a server or its firewall refuses your load test (429 "too many requests", 403), the report now says so plainly, shows when it started and at what load, and stops praising response times that were really just fast error replies. Peak requests per second and average users are now measured correctly — older reports are corrected when you open them.
  • About and Check for updates. See your version, check for a new one, and open your data folder — from "Version … · About" at the bottom of the sidebar.
  • Practice API: create an order (POST /orders) and fetch it (GET /orders/{id}) to try passing values safely.

Already on 0.3.0 or 0.3.1? The app updates itself (installer version) — just restart when it asks.

• HTML report matches your report. The exported HTML report now shows the same widgets, in the same order, as your report view, plus a short written debrief: what went well, what to look at, and what to try next. It is a single file that opens in any browser.
  • New app icon. The taskbar, Start menu, and installer show the APITestCenter logo instead of the default one.
  • Help bubbles no longer get cut off at the edge of a card.
  • Usage counts: no means no. If you say no to usage counts, the app stops counting entirely and deletes any counts it was keeping. Details: https://apitestcenter.com/privacy.html

Already on 0.3.0? The app offers this update by itself (installer version); just restart when it asks. Coming from 0.2.0? Download and install this version once.

• Import from Postman and OpenAPI. Bring in Postman collections and environments, or OpenAPI 3 / Swagger 2 files (JSON or YAML). Folders, auth, bodies, and variables come along; anything that can't is listed first.
  • Single-number tiles and section headings. Put one big number anywhere on a report, group charts under headings, and try the new By topic view (Speed, Reliability, Load). Eight more numbers to choose from, in the order you pick.
  • Formatted email report. Copy a designed summary into Outlook or Gmail, or download an email draft (.eml) with the full report attached.
  • Updates. The installed app now checks for new versions and offers to restart into them. (Portable and macOS show a download link.)
  • Optional usage counts. The app asks once whether to share anonymous counts. Say no and nothing is sent. Details: https://apitestcenter.com/privacy.html
  • macOS and Linux previews (when attached below). Not yet signed: on macOS, right-click the app and choose Open the first time.

Coming from 0.2.0? Download and install this version once; after that, updates arrive by themselves.
The first public release of APITestCenter — load testing you can actually read.
